header:
Date: 2028-01-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Patel (Redwood SE), Aaron Miles (DeckBridge Head of ML), Priya Nair (DeckBridge Platform Lead), Tom Reynolds (DeckBridge Finance)
summary: Product walkthrough of Redwood Console focused on usage analytics, per-route dashboards, and cost breakdown. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for production inference, wants clarity on per-route unit economics and auditability for finance and security. Agreed to run a pilot benchmark and exchange security docs.
topics: Batching & KV cache impact on economics
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros - I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Luca's our SE.
[00:08] Aaron Miles: Hey, Aaron here - head of ML at DeckBridge. Priya and Tom from platform and finance.
[00:15] Priya Nair: Hi all.
[00:18] Luca Patel: Great. Today we wanted to show the console dashboards — specifically how route-level usage and cost breakdowns look and how you can map those to your teams.
[00:28] Tom Reynolds: From finance perspective we'll be focused on per-route spend and predictability.
[00:33] Maya Chen: Perfect. Quick qualification — Aaron, what does your current stack look like for inference? Are you mostly self-hosted or using cloud endpoints?
[00:42] Aaron Miles: We're hybrid. We have some on-prem GPUs for sensitive stuff and then we also push to cloud instances during peak. Right now cost is fragmented, we don't have a single source of truth for token-level cost per route.
[00:56] Priya Nair: Also need tenant-level attribution because different product teams own routes.
[01:02] Luca Patel: Understood. That maps well to Redwood's per-route tagging and attribution features. I'll share my screen — console.home -> Usage -> Routes.
[01:15] [01:15] Luca Patel (screen share): You can see the route list on the left, filter by service, and then the central panel shows tokens, median latency, error rates and cost per thousand tokens. Notice the ability to group by team tag.
[01:31] Aaron Miles: Is that cost a modeled cost or the actual invoice?
[01:35] Luca Patel: Good question — it's modeled from token usage, model variant, and hardware profile. We provide a raw token cost and an allocation-adjusted cost; you can upload committed capacity pricing for Dedicated which will change the unit economics.
[01:48] Maya Chen: For payroll, eh sorry, for finance accuracy, you can map to actual billing via our billing exports too. We export CSVs and there's a billing API.
[01:58] Tom Reynolds: And retention? We need audit logs for 13 months.
[02:02] Maya Chen: We have audit logs and usage retention tiers. For enterprise customers the 13 month retention is supported via the enterprise plan and you can push logs to your S3 or the SIEM. I'll include the security pack link after the call.
[02:15] Priya Nair: Can you show an example of a high-cardinality route that has many short requests vs a batchable route?
[02:22] Luca Patel: Sure. Selecting route: 'search-autocomplete' — you'll see a pattern: high QPS, short responses. The console shows percentile latency and a breakdown of tokens per call. Now 'doc-summarize' — lower QPS, much higher average tokens.
[02:38] [02:38] Luca Patel: Here's the per-route cost waterfall — model cost, GPU time premium, and network. We also show 'batching efficiency' which is our estimate of savings from batching and KV cache reuse.
[02:49] Aaron Miles: That batching efficiency number — is it based on observed distribution or a theoretical best-case?
[02:54] Luca Patel: Observed. It's driven by your sequence length histogram and concurrency. For example, routes with very similar short inputs get high batching savings.
[03:03] Maya Chen: And for routes where you need deterministic latency we suggest dedicated pools or latency-first routing to keep tail latency low. There's a tradeoff: cost per token is higher on dedicated low-latency pools.
[03:15] Tom Reynolds: Can you quantify "higher"? Finance needs numbers to evaluate.
[03:19] Luca Patel: Typical difference depends on workload — for small chat-like requests, dedicated with reserved capacity can be 10-25% cheaper per token at high utilization because GC/packing is more efficient, but if you have spiky low-util workloads hosted burst pricing might be cheaper short-term. We'll produce a tailored model for DeckBridge.
[03:37] Aaron Miles: We're also concerned about data residency for user uploads — some models must run on-prem.
[03:42] Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports VPC or on-prem deployments and you can control key management (KMS/HSM). We'll include the on-prem checklist. 
[03:50] Priya Nair: How do rollouts work? We want canary for a new summarization model and quick fallback if latency regresses.
[03:56] Luca Patel: Console > Deployments. You can do canaries, A/B, or traffic-split by route. There's health checks and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if error rates spike.
[04:07] [04:07] Luca Patel: Now drilling into telemetry — here's a route's time-series for tokens and cost per minute. You can zoom into a spike and the console surfaces underlying requests and sample payloads (redacted).
[04:20] Aaron Miles: Are sample payloads stored? We can't store PII.
[04:24] Maya Chen: By default we redact sensitive fields; customers can set redaction rules. We also support no-storage modes where only metrics are kept and payloads are never persisted.
[04:34] Tom Reynolds: The spend allocation — can we get a per-feature chargeback report?
[04:38] Luca Patel: Yes — you can tag routes by team or feature and then produce monthly chargeback exports. There's even a forecast tool that extrapolates spend given your expected QPS and model mix.
[04:50] Aaron Miles: Great. On the topic of model mix — we saw notes about quantized variants. Does console show quality tradeoffs?
[04:57] Luca Patel: We integrate with Redwood Optimize. For each route you can link an eval set; Optimize recommends quantization levels and shows estimated latency/cost savings and a quality delta.
[05:08] Priya Nair: That sounds useful. We'd want to run the eval on our prompts.
[05:12] Maya Chen: We'll include steps to onboard your eval set. For the pilot we'll run your 'doc-summarize' prompt set so Optimize can recommend quantization and batching configs.
[05:21] [05:21] Aaron Miles: Question from my side — we have an SSO requirement and roles need to map to GitHub teams.
[05:26] Maya Chen: We support SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning; RBAC maps roles to teams and you can grant route-level permissions.
[05:34] Tom Reynolds: Any mention of external auditors or SOC2 evidence we can hand to our compliance team?
[05:39] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll send the SOC2 summary and the pen test attestation. Expect a link in the follow-up.
[05:46] Priya Nair: Can you show the billing export quick?
[05:49] Luca Patel: Sure — Export -> Billing CSV. Fields: route_id, team_tag, tokens_used, model_variant, cost_model, computed_cost. You can ingest into your FinOps tool.
[06:02] Aaron Miles: When you say 'computed_cost' is it mutable? If we upload committed capacity discounts will computed_cost change?
[06:08] Luca Patel: Yes, computed_cost recalculates with committed pricing or reserved capacity details.
[06:12] Maya Chen: Also you'll want to look at the utilization heatmap for your dedicated capacity; it helps you decide commit levels.
[06:20] [06:20] Luca Patel: I'm switching to the 'Route comparison' view — shows normalized cost per 1k tokens across models. You can overlay latency SLOs.
[06:29] Aaron Miles: This will help prioritize which routes to move to dedicated.
[06:33] Tom Reynolds: On contract terms — do you have minimum commitments for Dedicated?
[06:36] Maya Chen: Yes. Dedicated is monthly/annual commit. We'll propose a few tiers in the pricing worksheet. There's also a burst option for occasional spikes.
[06:46] Priya Nair: For the pilot, what infra do you need from us?
[06:49] Luca Patel: We'll need sample routes, representative prompt sets, and temporary credentials to hit a test endpoint. If you want VPC, we'll coordinate network peering.
[06:59] Aaron Miles: We'll share route list and histogram of sequence lengths.
[07:02] Maya Chen: Awesome. We'll kick off the pilot with a 2-hour benchmark in us-west-2, run both hosted and dedicated variants to give apples-to-apples economics.
[07:11] Tom Reynolds: Can you generate an ROI projection?
[07:14] Maya Chen: Yes. We'll take your QPS, model mix, and provide a 12-month projection with and without committed capacity.
[07:21] [07:21] Aaron Miles: A few quick clarifications — latency SLO is 200ms p95 for autocomplete; for summarization we accept up to 1.2s p95.
[07:31] Luca Patel: Noted. We'll set those SLOs in the pilot config.
[07:35] Priya Nair: About logs — do you support pushing traces to Datadog?
[07:39] Maya Chen: Yes, we have integrations for Datadog, Splunk, and New Relic.
[07:44] Tom Reynolds: Any competitors with better route attribution?
[07:47] Maya Chen: Some providers show costs at endpoint level only; Redwood focuses on per-route and per-team attribution with built-in FinOps exports.
[07:55] [07:55] Aaron Miles: Ok thanks. That was helpful.
[07:58] Luca Patel: Last bit — here's a sample exported CSV and the pricing worksheet template: https://redwood.app/links/deckbridge-pricing and the security pack: https://redwood.app/links/security-pack.
[08:11] Maya Chen: Next steps recap: we'll send security docs, pricing worksheet, and schedule a 2-hour pilot. Any other questions?
[08:18] Priya Nair: None from me.
[08:20] Tom Reynolds: Nope.
[08:21] Aaron Miles: Good.
[08:23] Maya Chen: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invite for the pilot and the artifacts.
[08:28] [08:28] Meeting ends.

Notes: occasional word recognition errors in the transcription (e.g., 'GC/packing' transcribed as 'G C packing'), speaker diarization may not be perfect; timestamps are approximate and appear every 30-90 seconds per natural pauses.
